articles.title: Sloth — the lazy task triager (local Gemma does your organizing)
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3 Sloth is a tiny CLI that takes your messy brain-dump — half-formed tasks, notes, random thoughts, copy-pasted reminders — and…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3 What I Built Sloth is a tiny CLI that takes your messy brain-dump — half-formed tasks, notes, random thoughts, copy-pasted reminders — and hands back a short, prioritized action plan with time estimates and one "do this first" pick. The pitch is one line: dump your brain, Sloth sorts it. You never organize; the sloth does. It was built for Week 3's theme, Slow and Steady : software that rewards laziness. October 20 is International Sloth Day, and honestly, the sloths have it figured out — conserve energy, move at your own pace, let something else do the work. Who would pay for this? Freelancers and students drowning in scattered to-dos — the same people who pay $10/month for AI organizers.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built I built NirvanaPilot , an ambient, non-intrusive VS Code Extension integrated with GitHub Copilot Chat that acts as the "subconscious mind" of your codebase. Honoring the essence of International Sloth Day, NirvanaPilot consumes 0% CPU while you are actively coding. However, the exact millisecond you take a break (15 seconds of complete typing inactivity), it wakes up in the background to scan your local repository for uncommitted drifts ( git diff ).

articles.title: The Poisson Distribution: Football Prediction’s Most Overrated “Mathematically Correct” Tool
articles.excerpt: If you've read any football prediction tutorial, you've seen this formula: P(goals = k) = λᵏ · e⁻ᵏ / k! It's called the Poisson distribution, born a hundred years ago to describe "how many phone calls…
articles.body: If you've read any football prediction tutorial, you've seen this formula: P(goals = k) = λᵏ · e⁻ᵏ / k! It's called the Poisson distribution, born a hundred years ago to describe "how many phone calls a telephone exchange receives per minute." Today, millions of people use it to predict football scores — and then, match after match of 3:3, 0:0, 4:2, they question their life choices. This article aims to explain it thoroughly: what Poisson does right, where it goes wrong on the football pitch, and why "mathematically correct" is precisely its biggest trap. 1. First, in plain language: what is the Poisson distribution? The math: Let X be the number of times an event occurs in a unit of time.

articles.body: Google has introduced a new co-creation workflow in Gemini Notebook for Slide Decks and Video Overviews. Rather than relying solely on an initial prompt or accepting an automatically generated result, users can select a focus topic, choose output settings, review a proposed plan and provide feedback before the final content is rendered. The change is designed to give people more control over source-based presentation and video content while retaining the speed of AI-assisted creation. According to Google's official announcement , the workflow can begin in chat or in Studio. Gemini Notebook can suggest topics based on uploaded sources, or users can enter a topic of their own. They can then guide the output by selecting its format, length, language and visual style.

articles.title: Keep your CLAUDE.md under 40 lines so Claude Code actually follows it
articles.excerpt: Most CLAUDE.md files I see grow into a wiki: architecture notes, style essays, a changelog, three pasted READMEs. Then people wonder why the agent ignores the one rule that mattered. CLAUDE.md is load…
articles.body: Most CLAUDE.md files I see grow into a wiki: architecture notes, style essays, a changelog, three pasted READMEs. Then people wonder why the agent ignores the one rule that mattered. CLAUDE.md is loaded into context at the start of a session, so every line competes with your actual task. Short, concrete house rules beat long explanations. A shape that works # House rules ## Before you edit - Read the file and its tests before changing it. - Ask before adding a new dependency. ## Commands - Test: `npm test` - Lint: `npm run lint -- --fix` - Never run: `git push --force` , `rm -rf` , database migrations. ## Done means - Tests and lint pass locally. - You list the files you changed and why, in one line each. ## Style - Match the surrounding code. No drive-by refactors.

articles.title: 8 Classic PlayStation Adventure Games that are Barely Playable Today
articles.excerpt: From Tomb Raider to Silent Hill, eight classic PlayStation games whose tank controls, cameras, or lost code make them hard to play today
articles.body: If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

articles.body: Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20). The JAXA ( Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency )-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 19, 2016: Europe's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli lander arrive at Mars
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli arrived at Mars! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars ! ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars , and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity.

articles.title: The moon is shrinking. 10,000 cracks on the lunar surface reveal by how much
articles.excerpt: One new study shows how much the moon has diminished over time.
articles.body: The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years. The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process . Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting. In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface.

articles.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
articles.excerpt: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment remini…
articles.body: What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
